claims.text: A hybrid of rapid laser scanning calorimetry, in-situ high-speed structural probes, and CALPHAD can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase properties across homogeneous high-entropy alloys.
Polycrystalline, single-phase HEAs can be prepared by conventional methods such as arc melting or laser powder bed fusion.
Laser-induced heating rates on the order of 10^3–10^5 K/s are suitable for the proposed measurements.
Calorimetric data and high-speed X-ray diffraction can be recorded simultaneously during transient HEA melting.
The transient thermal response can be used to calibrate a CALPHAD framework against experimental constants.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during laser-based processing or testing.
The approach is applicable to predominantly single-phase BCC, FCC, or eutectic HEA systems with minimized segregation and an adequate CALPHAD database.
Real-time diffraction can track atomic ordering and phase-transformation kinetics during melting.
The real-time structural observations can calibrate a thermodynamic model for fusion and liquid-phase properties.
Rapid laser heating minimizes non-equilibrium effects and enables near-equilibrium melting conditions to be captured.
Real-time structural data directly reveal melting, phase coalescence, and atomic rearrangements.
CALPHAD can interpolate fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and liquid properties from known elemental interactions.
The hybrid method will determine fusion-related properties with errors below 5% relative to conventional DSC and drop calorimetry.
The hybrid method will dramatically reduce measurement time while retaining consistent quantitative results.
Traditional DSC and drop calorimetry often require 10–20 hours per sample.
Traditional DSC and drop calorimetry do not easily capture transient structural evolution.
Severe segregation or multiphase behavior during melting makes CALPHAD calibration less reliable.
Extremely rapid solidification and non-equilibrium phases can limit the method's accuracy.
Prior refractory and eutectic HEA studies support the feasibility of capturing rapid transient thermal and structural data.
A systematic deviation greater than ±5% across multiple HEA compositions relative to conventional measurements would falsify the proposed approach.

contradictions.description: The applicability statement groups eutectic systems with predominantly single-phase behavior, while the boundary statement says multiphase behavior limits reliability; eutectic systems are not clearly reconciled with that restriction.

Rapid heating is asserted to suppress non-equilibrium effects and provide near-equilibrium melting, whereas extremely rapid processing and non-equilibrium phases are also identified as accuracy limitations; no rate-dependent boundary separating these regimes is supplied.
